# Task 1: Slate Health Check

**Data preparation.** I kept released films with a release date. Budgets of 0 or below \$1,000 and revenues of 0 are placeholders for "unknown", so I set them to missing. ROI = revenue / budget (ROI = 1 means revenue equals budget). Dollars are nominal.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(gt)
library(patchwork)

movies <- read_csv("data/movies.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(status == "Released", !is.na(release_year)) |>
  mutate(
    budget_m = if_else(budget >= 1000, budget / 1e6, NA_real_),
    roi = if_else(budget >= 1000 & revenue > 0, revenue / budget, NA_real_),
    log_budget = log10(budget_m),
    log_roi = log10(roi),
    period = if_else(release_year < 1990, 1985, floor(release_year / 5) * 5)  # 1985 = up to 1989
  )

movies_budget <- movies |> filter(!is.na(budget_m))
movies_roi <- movies |> filter(!is.na(roi))
```

## (a) Summary table

```{r}
summ <- function(x, name) {
  tibble(variable = name, n = length(x), missing = nrow(movies) - length(x),
         mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x), min = min(x), q1 = quantile(x, 0.25),
         median = median(x), q3 = quantile(x, 0.75), max = max(x))
}

bind_rows(summ(movies_budget$budget_m, "Budget ($M)"), summ(movies_roi$roi, "ROI")) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(mean, sd, min, q1, median, q3, max), decimals = 2)

count(movies, franchise_status)
```

Both variables are extremely right-skewed (mean budget \$37.4M vs median \$24.0M; mean ROI 11.1 vs median 2.3, driven by a few micro-budget hits), so I use medians and log10 scales. About 22% of films have no usable budget and 33% no usable ROI. Only 5.4% of films (260) are Franchise.

## (b) Distributions and genres

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.4
genre_data <- movies_roi |>
  filter(!is.na(primary_genre)) |>
  add_count(primary_genre) |>
  filter(n >= 20)                                   # genres with at least 20 films

p1 <- ggplot(movies_budget, aes(x = log_budget)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + labs(x = "log10 budget ($M)", y = "Films") + theme_minimal()
p2 <- movies_roi |> filter(roi >= 0.01) |> ggplot(aes(x = log_roi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") + labs(x = "log10 ROI (dashed: ROI = 1)", y = NULL) + theme_minimal()

g1 <- ggplot(genre_data, aes(x = log_budget, y = primary_genre)) + geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.5) + labs(x = "log10 budget ($M)", y = NULL) + theme_minimal()
g2 <- ggplot(genre_data, aes(x = log_roi, y = primary_genre)) + geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.5) + labs(x = "log10 ROI", y = NULL) + theme_minimal() + theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())
g3 <- genre_data |> group_by(primary_genre) |> summarise(prop_franchise = mean(franchise_status == "Franchise")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = prop_franchise, y = primary_genre)) + geom_col() + labs(x = "Proportion Franchise", y = NULL) + theme_minimal() + theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())

(p1 + p2) / (g1 + g2 + g3) + plot_layout(heights = c(1, 2))
```

Budget and ROI are roughly bell-shaped on the log scale; about 24% of films earned less than their budget (27 films with ROI below 0.01, likely data errors, are omitted from the ROI histogram). **Budget varies a lot by genre** (median: Animation \$76M, Adventure \$60M, Action \$44M vs Drama \$18M, Horror \$11M, Documentary \$2.5M), but **ROI is far more similar** (medians mostly 2--3; Horror highest at 3.7), so expensive genres are not rewarded with proportionally higher returns. Franchise films are concentrated in Horror (21%), Science Fiction (16%) and Action (11%), and almost absent from Drama and Documentary.

## (c) Has the slate shifted over time?

```{r}
#| fig-height: 1.7
period_summary <- movies |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(
    median_budget = median(budget_m[!is.na(budget_m)]),
    median_roi = median(roi[!is.na(roi)]),
    pct_franchise = 100 * mean(franchise_status == "Franchise")
  )

t1 <- ggplot(period_summary, aes(x = period, y = median_budget)) + geom_line() + geom_point() + labs(x = "5-year block", y = "Median budget ($M)") + theme_minimal()
t2 <- ggplot(period_summary, aes(x = period, y = median_roi)) + geom_line() + geom_point() + labs(x = "5-year block", y = "Median ROI") + theme_minimal()
t3 <- ggplot(period_summary, aes(x = period, y = pct_franchise)) + geom_line() + geom_point() + labs(x = "5-year block", y = "% Franchise") + theme_minimal()

t1 + t2 + t3
```

Each point is a 5-year block (1985 = films up to 1989; 2015 = 2015 onwards, partial). The **median budget jumped from about \$6M (up to 1989) to \$25--30M in the 1990s and has stayed at \$25M since 2005**, so it has fallen in real terms. The median ROI was about 2.0 from the mid-1990s and has risen to 2.8 by 2015+ (the pre-1990 value of 4.8 is probably inflated because only successful older films have revenue recorded). The trend to watch is that the **franchise share has roughly doubled since 2005--09** (3.9%) to 11.6% in 2015+.

## (d) Summary for the Head of Production

The file holds 4,803 films; I analysed the 4,794 that were released and dated. Unknown budgets and revenues are stored as 0 or tiny numbers, so I treated them as missing (about one in five films has no usable budget, one in three no usable ROI); results describe films with recorded figures only.

A typical film costs about \$24M (middle half: \$9M--\$50M) and earns about 2.3 times its budget, but one in four earned less than it cost. Budgets differ much more by genre than returns do, and only about 5% of films are Franchise. The typical budget has been flat at about \$25M since the mid-2000s, median returns have crept up, and the franchise share has roughly doubled to about 12%, which is worth monitoring.

# Task 2: Franchise vs. Original: Investment Strategy

Leadership's concern is that (i) Originals are mostly small and cheap while Franchise films have much larger budgets, and (ii) Franchise films generate most of the revenue. I use the cleaned data from Task 1. The Franchise label is taken as given, but it looks narrow: all 94 films with a "sequel" keyword are Franchise, yet *The Avengers* and *The Dark Knight Rises* are labelled Original.

## (a) Comparing the full budget distributions

```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.2
p_density <- ggplot(movies_budget, aes(x = log_budget, fill = franchise_status)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(x = "log10 budget ($M): 1 = $10M, 2 = $100M", y = "Density", fill = "Group") +
  theme_minimal()

p_box <- ggplot(movies_budget, aes(x = franchise_status, y = log_budget)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "log10 budget ($M)") +
  theme_minimal()

p_density + p_box

movies |>
  group_by(franchise_status) |>
  summarise(
    films = n(),
    n_budget = sum(!is.na(budget_m)),
    median_budget = median(budget_m[!is.na(budget_m)]),
    n_over_100M = sum(budget_m[!is.na(budget_m)] >= 100),
    median_roi = median(roi[!is.na(roi)]),
    prop_roi_below_1 = mean(roi[!is.na(roi)] < 1),
    total_revenue = sum(revenue)
  ) |>
  mutate(revenue_share = total_revenue / sum(total_revenue)) |>
  select(-total_revenue) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(median_budget, median_roi), decimals = 1) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = c(prop_roi_below_1, revenue_share), decimals = 1)
```

**Similarities:** both distributions are right-skewed with one main peak on the log scale and a very wide range (under \$1M to over \$250M), and they overlap heavily. **Differences:** the Franchise distribution is shifted right (median \$40M vs \$22M, about 1.8 times); Franchise films rarely have very small budgets, and a larger share are very expensive (56 of 233, 24%, at \$100M or more vs 264 of 3,498, 7.5%). However, because Originals are so numerous, there are **more Original films at \$100M or more (264) than Franchise films (56)**.

## (b) 95% interval for the difference in median budget

The median has no simple standard error and budgets are skewed, so I used a bootstrap: resample each group's budgets separately with replacement (keeping its size), compute median(Franchise) − median(Original), repeat 10,000 times, and take the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles.

```{r}
f <- movies_budget |> filter(franchise_status == "Franchise") |> pull(budget_m)
o <- movies_budget |> filter(franchise_status == "Original") |> pull(budget_m)

set.seed(2420)
boot_diff <- map_dbl(1:10000, ~ median(sample(f, replace = TRUE)) - median(sample(o, replace = TRUE)))

c(observed = median(f) - median(o), quantile(boot_diff, probs = c(0.025, 0.975)))
```

The median Franchise budget is **\$18.0M higher than the median Original budget (95% bootstrap interval roughly \$9M to \$26M)**, about 1.8 times as large. The interval is far from 0, so the gap is not sampling noise; it is wide because there are only 233 Franchise films.

## (c) Does the evidence support leadership's concern?

**Part (i) is partly supported.** Franchise films are clearly more expensive at the median, but "mostly small and low-budget" overstates it: the distributions overlap strongly and Originals include many large productions (264 at \$100M or more). Part of the gap is genre mix, as Franchise films sit in expensive genres (Task 1b). Originals are also more often missing a usable budget (23% vs 10%), and these are plausibly small films, so the true Original median is probably even lower.

**Part (ii) is not supported.** Franchise films are 5.4% of the slate but bring in only **14.2% of total revenue**; 85.8% comes from Originals. Per film, Franchise films are much more valuable (median ROI 3.4 vs 2.2; only 5.9% earn less than their budget vs 25.8% of Originals), but there are too few to dominate. Because the label is narrow, the true franchise share of revenue is probably higher and should be rechecked.

## (d) Advice for the next decade

Franchise films earn higher and safer returns per dollar, so they should remain a stable core of the slate rather than be cut to fund originals. But Originals produce most of the revenue, have a median ROI of 2.2 (well above 1), and there are many big-budget Originals, so a push for more originals is financially defensible. I would **expand originals gradually**, putting new greenlights mainly on low-to-mid budgets (below about \$30M) where the absolute downside is limited, keeping a few larger original bets, and reviewing ROI every few years to check that the new originals earn returns like the historical ones. Caveats: ROI is gross revenue over production budget (excluding marketing and the cinemas' share), so an ROI near 2 is close to break-even in practice; only released films are observed; dollars are nominal; and none of this shows that being Original or Franchise *causes* a film's return.

**Summary for the Head of Production / Finance.** Franchise films do cost more: a typical Franchise film has a budget of about \$40M versus \$22M for an Original, and the gap is real (roughly \$9M to \$26M with 95% confidence). But the picture is less one-sided than leadership assumes. Originals are about 95% of the slate and bring in about 86% of revenue, and there are more original films above \$100M than franchise ones. Franchise films earn more per film and per dollar, so they should stay a reliable core. We recommend growing original projects gradually, starting with modest budgets, tracking their returns, and re-running this analysis with a broader definition of "franchise", since the current label misses well-known series.

# Task 3: Modelling Budgets & Downside Risk

## 3a Modelling Universal Pictures’ production budgets

```{r}
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)

movies <- read_csv("data/movies.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

universal_budget <- movies |>
  filter(
    primary_company == "Universal Pictures",
    is.finite(budget),
    budget >= 10000
  ) |>
  mutate(budget_millions = budget / 1e6)

# Check the filtered data
universal_budget |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    min_budget = min(budget),
    median_budget = median(budget),
    mean_budget = mean(budget),
    max_budget = max(budget)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-t3-budget-dist
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of production budgets for Universal Pictures films."
ggplot(universal_budget, aes(x = budget_millions)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 25,
    fill = "skyblue",
    colour = "white"
  ) +
  geom_density(colour = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Budget Distribution of Universal Pictures Films",
    x = "Budget (US$ millions)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
universal_budget |>
  summarise(
    skewness = mean(
      (budget_millions - mean(budget_millions))^3
    ) / sd(budget_millions)^3
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t3-aic
#| tbl-cap: "AIC comparison of candidate models for Universal Pictures production budgets."
library(fitdistrplus)

budget <- universal_budget$budget_millions

fit_normal <- fitdist(budget, "norm")
fit_lognormal <- fitdist(budget, "lnorm")
fit_gamma <- fitdist(budget, "gamma")

aic_results <- tibble(
  Distribution = c("Normal", "Log-normal", "Gamma"),
  AIC = c(
    fit_normal$aic,
    fit_lognormal$aic,
    fit_gamma$aic
  )
) |>
  arrange(AIC)

knitr::kable(aic_results, digits = 1)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-t3-budget-qq
#| fig-cap: "Q–Q plots comparing normal, log-normal and gamma models for Universal Pictures production budgets."
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))

qqcomp(
  fit_normal,
  main = "Normal"
)

qqcomp(
  fit_lognormal,
  main = "Log-normal"
)

qqcomp(
  fit_gamma,
  main = "Gamma"
)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

After excluding invalid and placeholder budget values below US\$10,000, 243 Universal Pictures films remained. The budget distribution (@fig-t3-budget-dist) was positively skewed, with a sample skewness of 1.57, suggesting that a symmetric normal distribution may be unsuitable.

Three candidate distributions were fitted: normal, log-normal and gamma. The gamma distribution achieved the lowest AIC (2320.1), compared with 2349.2 for the log-normal distribution and 2454.1 for the normal distribution (@tbl-t3-aic). The Q–Q plots (@fig-t3-budget-qq) also suggest that the gamma model provides the closest overall fit, although some deviations remain in the upper tail. Therefore, among the three candidates, the gamma distribution is the preferred model for describing Universal Pictures film budgets.

## 3b Estimating the 25th percentile of Action ROI

```{r}
films |>
  summarise(
    total_rows = n(),
    has_genre = "primary_genre" %in% names(films),
    has_budget = "budget" %in% names(films),
    has_revenue = "revenue" %in% names(films)
  )
```

```{r}
action_films <- movies |>
  filter(
    primary_genre == "Action",
    is.finite(budget),
    budget >= 10000,
    is.finite(revenue),
    revenue > 0
  ) |>
  mutate(roi_calc = revenue / budget) |>
  filter(is.finite(roi_calc))

action_films |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    roi_q25 = quantile(roi_calc, 0.25),
    roi_median = median(roi_calc),
    roi_min = min(roi_calc),
    roi_max = max(roi_calc)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t3-roi-ci
#| tbl-cap: "Estimated 25th percentile of Action-film ROI and 95% confidence intervals."
set.seed(2420)

# Point estimate
q25_hat <- quantile(action_films$roi_calc, 0.25)

# Method 1: Bootstrap percentile interval
B <- 5000

boot_q25 <- replicate(B, {
  boot_sample <- sample(
    action_films$roi_calc,
    size = nrow(action_films),
    replace = TRUE
  )
  quantile(boot_sample, 0.25)
})

boot_ci <- quantile(boot_q25, c(0.025, 0.975))

# Method 2: Order-statistic interval
x <- sort(action_films$roi_calc)
n <- length(x)

alpha <- 0.05
lower_index <- qbinom(alpha / 2, n, 0.25)
upper_index <- qbinom(1 - alpha / 2, n, 0.25) + 1

# Keep indices within valid sample positions
lower_index <- max(1, lower_index)
upper_index <- min(n, upper_index)

order_ci <- c(
  lower = x[lower_index],
  upper = x[upper_index]
)

# Display results
tibble(
  Method = c("Bootstrap percentile", "Order statistic"),
  Estimate = rep(as.numeric(q25_hat), 2),
  `Lower 95% CI` = c(boot_ci[1], order_ci[1]),
  `Upper 95% CI` = c(boot_ci[2], order_ci[2])
) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

For Action films across all studios, the estimated 25th percentile of ROI was 0.907. The bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval was \[0.798, 1.052\], while the order-statistic interval was \[0.794, 1.072\]. Both methods produced the same point estimate, with the order-statistic interval slightly wider. The results suggest that the lower quartile of Action-film ROI is close to 1, although uncertainty remains around this benchmark.

## 3c Comparison of the percentile estimators

Both methods estimate the 25th percentile as 0.907 and give similar 95% confidence intervals (@tbl-t3-roi-ci). The order-statistic interval is slightly wider. The bootstrap method resamples the observed films, whereas the order-statistic method uses ranked observations and binomial probabilities to obtain interval bounds. Both intervals include 1, so the population lower quartile could lie on either side of the production-budget recoupment benchmark.

## 3d Recommendation for Finance

For the budget simulator, we recommend the gamma distribution for Universal Pictures’ production budgets because it has the lowest AIC among the three candidates and is supported by the Q–Q diagnostics. This model provides a historical benchmark rather than a guarantee of Meridian’s future cost structure.

For the Action slate, Finance should plan around a lower-quartile ROI of approximately 0.91: about one quarter of films in the observed sample earned less than 91 cents in worldwide box-office revenue per dollar of production budget. The two 95% confidence intervals are approximately 0.80–1.05 and 0.79–1.07, indicating uncertainty around the 1x production-budget recoupment benchmark. This figure describes the lower quarter of the observed revenue-to-budget ratios and should not be interpreted as a prediction for an individual film. ROI is calculated using reported worldwide box-office revenue and production budget; it does not account for marketing, distribution or other costs. Missing financial records and the historical nature of the sample should also be considered when applying these findings to future greenlighting decisions.

# Task 4: Building a Greenlight Risk Model

## 4a Outcome and sample

A flop has worldwide box-office revenue below production budget (ROI < 1). Logistic regression models a binary outcome with probabilities in [0,1]; linear regression does not constrain probabilities, and Poisson regression models counts. We exclude placeholder financials, restrict releases to 2016 or earlier and five focus genres, and use complete predictors. A stratified 80/20 split separates training from evaluation.

```{r}
#| label: t4-data
#| echo: true
library(brms)
t4_data <- readr::read_csv("data/movies.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::filter(release_year <= 2016, budget >= 10000, revenue > 0) |>
  dplyr::mutate(flop = as.integer(revenue / budget < 1), log_budget = log(budget),
    primary_genre = factor(primary_genre), cast_10 = cast_size / 10,
    franchise_status = factor(franchise_status, c("Original", "Franchise"))) |>
  tidyr::drop_na(primary_genre, franchise_status, log_budget, cast_size) |>
  dplyr::filter(primary_genre %in% c("Action", "Comedy", "Drama", "Horror", "Animation")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(primary_genre = relevel(droplevels(primary_genre), "Drama"))
set.seed(24205242)
t4_ids <- t4_data |> dplyr::group_by(flop) |> dplyr::slice_sample(prop = .8) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |> dplyr::pull(id)
t4_train <- dplyr::filter(t4_data, id %in% t4_ids)
t4_test <- dplyr::filter(t4_data, !id %in% t4_ids)
```

The sample contains `r nrow(t4_data)` films (`r sum(t4_data$flop)` flops), with `r nrow(t4_train)` training and `r nrow(t4_test)` test films. Recorded cast size approximates planned cast size and must be estimated before greenlight. Models assume independent outcomes and additive linear effects of log budget and cast size on log-odds; related franchise films may violate independence.

## 4b Models and uncertainty

```{r}
#| label: t4-models
#| echo: true
#| cache: true
t4_formula <- flop ~ primary_genre + franchise_status + log_budget + cast_10
t4_freq <- glm(t4_formula, data = t4_train, family = binomial())
t4_bayes <- brm(t4_formula, data = t4_train, family = bernoulli(),
  prior = c(prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b"),
            prior(normal(0, 2.5), class = "Intercept")),
  chains = 4, iter = 4000, warmup = 1000, cores = 2, seed = 24205242, refresh = 0)
t4_fc <- coef(summary(t4_freq))[-1, , drop = FALSE]
t4_bc <- fixef(t4_bayes)[rownames(t4_fc), , drop = FALSE]
t4_fmt <- function(x, l, u) sprintf("%.2f (%.2f–%.2f)", x, l, u)
t4_draws <- posterior::as_draws_df(t4_bayes)
t4_pp <- mean(t4_draws$b_franchise_statusFranchise < 0)
t4_sp <- rstan::get_sampler_params(t4_bayes$fit, inc_warmup = FALSE)
t4_diag <- c(Rhat = max(posterior::summarise_draws(t4_draws)$rhat, na.rm = TRUE),
  Divergences = sum(sapply(t4_sp, function(x) sum(x[, "divergent__"]))),
  DepthHits = sum(sapply(t4_sp, function(x) sum(x[, "treedepth__"] >= 10))))
```

Priors are on log-odds: Normal(0,1) for slopes and Normal(0,2.5) for the internally centred intercept. The slope prior allows about 95% of odds ratios between 0.14 and 7.10 per unit. Four chains retain 12,000 draws; maximum R-hat is `r sprintf("%.3f", t4_diag["Rhat"])`, with `r t4_diag["Divergences"]` divergences and `r t4_diag["DepthHits"]` tree-depth hits.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t4-models
#| tbl-cap: "Adjusted odds ratios: frequentist 95% CI and Bayesian 95% CrI."
#| echo: true
knitr::kable(data.frame(Predictor = c("Action vs Drama", "Animation vs Drama",
  "Comedy vs Drama", "Horror vs Drama", "Franchise vs Original", "Log budget (+1)",
  "Cast (+10)"), Frequentist = t4_fmt(exp(t4_fc[,1]),
  exp(t4_fc[,1]-1.96*t4_fc[,2]), exp(t4_fc[,1]+1.96*t4_fc[,2])),
  Bayesian = t4_fmt(exp(t4_bc[,1]), exp(t4_bc[,3]), exp(t4_bc[,4]))))
```

Both models agree (@tbl-t4-models). Holding other predictors fixed, franchise status has OR 0.24 (CI 0.12–0.48) versus 0.27 (CrI 0.14–0.48); ten extra cast members have OR 0.81 under both models. These describe lower odds, not probability-point reductions or causal effects. All retained posterior draws have a negative franchise coefficient, suggesting a posterior probability close to 100% under the specified model and priors. Confidence intervals have repeated-sampling coverage; credible intervals express posterior uncertainty.

## 4c Held-out performance

We use the training flop proportion as a screening threshold, with 0.50 for comparison. This prioritises detecting minority-class flops without tuning on the test set; it is not an optimised business cost threshold.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t4-performance
#| tbl-cap: "Test performance (%); flop is positive; undefined precision is NA."
#| echo: true
t4_pf <- predict(t4_freq, t4_test, type = "response")
t4_pb <- colMeans(posterior_epred(t4_bayes, newdata = t4_test))
t4_cut <- mean(t4_train$flop)
t4_metrics <- function(p, cut) {
  y <- t4_test$flop; z <- p >= cut
  tp <- sum(z & y == 1); tn <- sum(!z & y == 0)
  fp <- sum(z & y == 0); fn <- sum(!z & y == 1)
  c(Accuracy = mean(z == y), Sensitivity = tp/(tp+fn),
    Specificity = tn/(tn+fp), Precision = if (tp+fp) tp/(tp+fp) else NA_real_)
}
t4_perf <- rbind(t4_metrics(t4_pf,.5), t4_metrics(t4_pf,t4_cut),
                 t4_metrics(t4_pb,.5), t4_metrics(t4_pb,t4_cut))
knitr::kable(data.frame(Model = rep(c("Frequentist","Bayesian"), each = 2),
  Threshold = rep(c(.5,t4_cut),2), round(100*t4_perf,1)), digits = c(0,3,1,1,1,1))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t4-confusion
#| tbl-cap: "Bayesian screening matrix: actual rows, predicted columns (0 = non-flop)."
#| echo: true
knitr::kable(table(Actual = t4_test$flop, Predicted = as.integer(t4_pb >= t4_cut)))
```

At 0.50 neither model flags flops; 74.6% accuracy matches always predicting non-flop. Bayesian screening detects 86/115 flops (74.8% sensitivity), but flags 181 non-flops; precision is 32.2%. Many flagged films therefore require further review. Results use one random split and do not guarantee future performance.

## 4d Pitches and management advice

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t4-pitches
#| tbl-cap: "Hypothetical pitches: mean flop probability and 95% credible interval."
#| echo: true
t4_pitches <- tibble::tibble(Pitch = c("Original horror","Original drama","Franchise action"),
  primary_genre = factor(c("Horror","Drama","Action"), levels(t4_train$primary_genre)),
  franchise_status = factor(c("Original","Original","Franchise"),
    levels(t4_train$franchise_status)), budget_m = c(10,25,80), cast_10 = c(1.5,2.5,4)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(log_budget = log(budget_m*1e6))
t4_pd <- posterior_epred(t4_bayes, newdata = t4_pitches)
knitr::kable(data.frame(Pitch = t4_pitches$Pitch, `Budget USD m` = t4_pitches$budget_m,
  Cast = 10*t4_pitches$cast_10, `Flop % (95% CrI)` = t4_fmt(100*colMeans(t4_pd),
    100*apply(t4_pd,2,quantile,.025), 100*apply(t4_pd,2,quantile,.975)),
  Recommendation = c("Conditional go","Hold for review","Conditional go"), check.names = FALSE))
```

**Management summary.** Provisionally support horror and franchise action; review the drama's costs and revenue assumptions. This is a screening aid with many false alarms, not an automatic rejection rule. Intervals describe uncertainty in estimated probabilities, not individual outcomes. Historical selection, franchise dependence and uncertain planned cast sizes limit generalisation. Worldwide box office is not studio receipts, and flop excludes marketing and distribution costs; lower flop risk does not guarantee profit or smaller financial exposure.
